title: Learning to See Together
headline: How Humility Changes the Way You See People
tagline: Compassion often begins where assumptions end.
seo_title: Humility and Difficult People: Philippians 2:3-4 Group Questions | TheWrkShop
seo_description: Pride assumes; humility becomes curious. Reflection and men's group discussion questions on Philippians 2:3-4 and seeing people as image-bearers.
verse_text: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

scriptures.text: Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves. Let each of you look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others.

items: Before asking, “How can I become more patient?”
perhaps ask, “Lord, help me see people the way You see them.”
Because patience often grows from perspective.
Think about someone who has been difficult for you recently.
- What might they be carrying today?
- What pressure are they under?
- What pain could be shaping their responses?
- What if I knew their whole story?
- How might Christ be inviting me to love them today?
Pride assumes.
Humility becomes curious.
Pride fills in the blanks.
Humility leaves room for grace.

blocks.text: Love asks questions before it forms conclusions.

items: Compassion often begins where assumptions end.
Grace often begins where certainty ends.
When we gather as brothers, we’re doing far more than studying information.
We’re learning to see.
One brother’s testimony strengthens another’s faith.
One brother’s struggle cultivates another’s compassion.
One brother’s perspective exposes another’s blind spot.
Together we begin seeing image-bearers instead of interruptions.
Neighbors instead of nuisances.
Souls instead of stereotypes.
People instead of projects.

blocks.text: As we behold Christ together…. we begin becoming more like Christ together.

items: Why do we naturally reduce people to labels instead of seeing them as image-bearers?
Who has been hardest for you to see through Christ’s eyes, and why?
How did Jesus consistently treat people that everyone else overlooked, avoided or rejected?
What changes in our relationships when we remember every person carries God’s image?
How does abiding in Christ reshape the way we interpret difficult people?
Who is God inviting you to see differently this week, and what is one practical way you can honor them?
